issues.item: Triggers: Female Presence: Being alone with women
issues.explanation: The trigger pattern is hard to reconcile with the stated trauma of physical abuse by a romantic partner. Being alone with women is not a plausible primary trigger for partner violence in a female patient unless there is additional trauma history not represented elsewhere, and military/police uniforms also suggest a different threat context that is not supported by the memory, threat, or appraisal items.

issues.item: Triggers: Visual (Uniforms): Military or police uniforms
issues.explanation: The memory/appraisal pattern centers on guilt and global identity damage, but the selected triggers point toward external threat cues unrelated to intimate-partner violence. This creates a cross-node mismatch: the triggers imply one trauma context, while memory and appraisals imply another.

issues.item: Memory: Guilt on Recall: When I remember the event I feel intense guilt
issues.explanation: 'I no longer belong anywhere' is not impossible, but in this profile it intensifies the mismatch because the appraisals are extremely global and identity-based while the trigger content is narrow and externally themed in ways not linked to the romantic-partner abuse formulation.

issues.item: Triggers: Visual (Uniforms): Military or police uniforms
issues.explanation: Military or police uniforms are not impossible as triggers after intimate partner physical abuse, but in this profile they are hard to justify because no other trigger, memory, threat, appraisal, or strategy item links the trauma to police/military involvement, authority figures, or uniformed responders. This makes the trigger feel disconnected from the rest of the formulation.

issues.item: Negative Appraisals: Shattered Beliefs: My beliefs about how the world works have been completely destroyed
issues.explanation: This item is not impossible, but alongside the more specific interpersonal/self-related profile (self-blame, guilt on recall, being alone with men, body-focused avoidance, belonging nowhere), a global 'completely destroyed' worldview reads broader than the rest of the node and may overstate the appraisal pattern relative to the otherwise relationship- and self-focused presentation.

issues.item: Threat: Risky Behavior: Taking too many risks or doing things that could cause you harm
issues.explanation: Risky behavior is hard to reconcile with the rest of the profile, which otherwise reflects fear, hypervigilance, avoidance, mistrust, and tension after intimate partner physical abuse. It pulls toward a more disinhibited presentation that is not supported by the trigger, memory, appraisal, or other strategy items.

issues.item: Maladaptive Strategies: Avoid Own Body: Paying attention to or looking at my own body
issues.explanation: 'Avoid Own Body' is weakly supported by the rest of the profile. The selected triggers, memories, threats, and appraisals center on interpersonal danger, guilt, and mistrust rather than body-focused trauma responses. This item is not impossible, but in this profile it appears disconnected from the main formulation compared with the other avoidance item.

vignette:
Leilani is a 20-year-old married woman of Pacific Islander background who works as an interior designer for a small residential firm. When she speaks about the relationship in which she was assaulted, she does not begin with a clear, orderly account. She starts, stops, apologizes, and loses the thread. There are moments when she says she knows what happened but cannot seem to hold the story together long enough to tell it straight through. What comes across most clearly is the atmosphere of those episodes: being alone with her partner in enclosed spaces, the sudden shift in his face and posture, the sound of his movements becoming louder, closer, and dangerous. Loud noises now strike her as if they belong to that same world. A door slamming in an apartment hallway, a dropped tool at a worksite, a man’s raised voice from the street can make her body tighten before she has even identified what she heard.

In the relationship, the abuse took place behind closed doors, often when no one else was around. That fact has remained painfully alive for her. Being alone in a room or building feels unsafe in a way she struggles to explain to other people, as though privacy itself has become threatening. She is especially uneasy if the person nearby is a man. If she arrives early to meet a male contractor at a client’s home and finds herself alone with him before others come, she feels her chest pull tight and her attention sharpen toward exits, footsteps, and any sudden movement. She knows these men are not the person who hurt her, yet being alone with men has become one of the most potent moments of alarm in her daily life.

After the relationship ended, she expected the fear to fade once she no longer had to see him. Instead, seeing the offender in person, or even catching sight of someone she thinks might be him from behind, jolts her instantly. She frequently looks behind her when walking to her car after site visits or when leaving the design studio, checking whether someone is following her. She describes herself as “always scanning.” Even in ordinary settings she sits where she can see entrances, notices male voices before anyone else seems to, and carries a constant physical readiness, shoulders tight, stomach clenched, as if her body is prepared for something to happen. She says it is exhausting, but relaxing feels foolish to her, because she has come to believe that people cannot be trusted and that danger arrives when you let your guard down.

Over the months that followed the abuse, her world became smaller. She began avoiding dark places because darkness feels too much like those moments when she could not read what was about to happen until it was already happening. At work she started turning down evening installations and last-minute client visits if she thought she might end up alone in a vacant property. She asks coworkers to stay nearby when possible and sometimes waits in her car rather than enter a building by herself. These decisions have affected how others see her reliability, and she is painfully aware of it. At home, she prefers not to be in a room by herself and moves from space to space to stay near her husband, though she feels ashamed needing that reassurance at her age.

Her thoughts about what happened are harsh and repetitive. She repeatedly blames herself, circling the same questions about what she missed, why she stayed, what she should have done differently. When memories surface, guilt floods in so intensely that it can feel bigger than the memory itself. Sometimes she does not even get a picture in her mind; instead, the emotional force arrives all at once—fear, shame, and guilt with no clear scene attached. She finds that especially unsettling, because it leaves her feeling overtaken by something she cannot fully describe. When friends or family have tried to ask what happened, she has often gone quiet or said she does not know how to explain it. Over time she has withdrawn from many of them. She feels that she no longer belongs anywhere, not fully with friends, not fully at work, not even fully in the ordinary life of a newly married young woman. She says there is a version of everyone else still moving forward, while her own life feels ruined, as though the abuse divided everything into before and after.

What brought Leilani to seek help now was a recent cluster of moments she could not dismiss: freezing when left alone with a male electrician on a renovation consult, startling so intensely at a crashing sample board in the studio that she had to step outside, and later spotting her former partner across a parking lot and spending the rest of the day checking over her shoulder. She came in frightened by how narrow her life has become and by how certain she feels that trust is no longer possible. At the same time, she is hoping for some way to speak about what happened without losing the thread, and to feel that being alone, at work or anywhere else, does not have to mean she is in danger again.
